summary:
Aim for puns where a single pivot word or phrase carries two complete, independently coherent readings — one literal to the topic, one figurative or idiomatic — and where both readings are actively anchored by the surrounding words rather than left implied. The strongest model puns ("groundbreaking" shovel, "lost interest" banker, "developed" photographic memory) work because the setup makes the literal reading inevitable while the idiom reading lands as the punchline simultaneously. Build toward that double-anchoring: choose a noun or scenario that forces the literal sense, then end on the pivot so the idiomatic sense snaps into place.

Pick pivots that are genuine polysemes or established idioms with a concrete physical origin — "fluke," "swell," "groundbreaking," "crossed a line," "developed." These give you two fully-formed meanings for free. Avoid pivots whose second reading is thin, generic, or merely evaluative ("stirring up trouble," "test of patience," "missed the point" in a classroom): the idiom is fine but the literal tie to the topic is weak, so the pun reads as a normal sentence with a faint wink rather than a genuine collision.

Avoid soundalike-only mechanics ("toe-tally," "hi/high") unless the substitution also yields a sentence that makes literal sense in its new form. Pure homophone swaps with no semantic payoff score low on ambiguity and surprise — they are puns the reader spots but does not enjoy. The "two tired" pattern is the floor, not the target.

Resist building the entire setup as context for a tacked-on idiom. If the sentence before the pivot only exists to justify the punchline, the pun feels lopsided. Instead, write setups that are interesting or specific on their own (the whale researcher, the anti-gravity book), so the pivot rewards a sentence the reader was already enjoying.

Keep cadence tight: one sentence, or two short clauses with a semicolon or period before the turn. Trim filler adjectives and throat-clearing. Match register to audience, but never sacrifice the dual reading for topical name-dropping — relevance without ambiguity is just a themed sentence.
